vignette:
He is 20, a young doctor from an African country, and when he first begins to talk about the war, he does it in fragments, as if each piece has to be lifted carefully from somewhere heavy. Before the fighting reaches his town, he is already working beyond what most people would expect from someone his age. He has finished medical training quickly in a system stretched by shortages, and he is proud of the white coat that makes older men call him “doctor” with a mixture of respect and urgency. He is single, living in a rented room near the hospital, sending money home when he can. He imagines a future in surgery, in exams, in a life built by steady effort.

Then the front line shifts.

At first the hospital changes in ways that seem almost manageable. Windows are taped. Supplies disappear faster than they arrive. The injured come in waves, then floods. He works for hours with blood drying on his sleeves, learning to sort who might live from who almost certainly will not. He tells himself to focus on tasks: airway, bleeding, pulse, pressure, stitch, compress, move on. The shelling sounds distant at first, like weather. Then one afternoon it lands close enough to shake dust from the ceiling and send everyone to the floor. He remembers the cry of a child somewhere down the corridor, and the terrible, disciplined way the staff stand back up and continue.

The worst night comes months later. Armed men and wounded soldiers arrive at nearly the same time. The generators fail twice. In the dark, lit by phones and one failing lamp, he tries to treat a teenage fighter whose abdomen is torn open. Outside, gunfire cracks so close that the walls seem to snap with it. Someone shouts that the compound is being overrun. A nurse beside him is hit when glass bursts inward. He still sees the look on her face—more surprise than pain—before she falls. People begin running. He does not remember deciding to run himself. He remembers stepping over bodies in the corridor, the sharp smell of blood and diesel, and the humiliating certainty that if he stops to help one more person he will die there too. He escapes through a rear entrance with two other staff members and spends the rest of the night hiding in a drainage ditch, his hands sticky with someone else’s blood, listening to bursts of gunfire and waiting to be found.

Afterward, he keeps moving. There is displacement, temporary shelters, then work again in another clinic because there is always work for a doctor in a war. On the outside he appears functional, even impressive. He is punctual, efficient, calm with patients. But the nights become hostile territory. He sleeps in short stretches and wakes soaked in sweat, hearing the pop of gunfire in the slam of a door or the backfire of a motorbike. In dreams he is back in the corridor, trying to carry everyone at once, always leaving someone behind. He dreads darkness and prefers to stay under fluorescent lights until exhaustion forces him to lie down.

He notices changes in himself that trouble him more than the fear. He has become watchful in a way that never switches off. In restaurants or waiting rooms he sits near exits and scans faces without meaning to. When people crowd behind him, his shoulders tense instantly. If he hears raised voices, his chest tightens and he is no longer fully in the present room. During one consultation, a patient’s relative drops a metal tray, and he flinches so violently that everyone stares. He laughs it off, but afterward he locks himself in the staff bathroom and shakes.

He avoids speaking about the hospital attack, especially with family. His mother tells him he is blessed to be alive, and he agrees, though privately he does not feel lucky. He feels accused by memory. He thinks of the nurse who was shot, the boy on the table, the patients he abandoned when he ran. He knows, in the rational language he uses for others, that no one person could have saved them. But in the quiet moments another voice says doctor, you left. That voice is hardest to bear.

Being single has made his life simpler and lonelier at once. Friends invite him out, but he often declines because noise, laughter, and unpredictability exhaust him. When he does go, he keeps his back to the wall and leaves early. He has stopped answering messages from a woman he once liked because he cannot imagine explaining why he goes cold when she touches him unexpectedly, or why he seems far away even when sitting beside her.

Now, in sessions, he speaks in a controlled tone that sometimes breaks without warning. He says he feels older than his age and ashamed of how frightened he still is. He continues to work as a doctor, and some days that role anchors him. On other days every stretcher, every siren, every smell of antiseptic opens a door he is trying not to walk through. He wants to be the kind of physician who can remain present with suffering. Instead, he often feels split in two: the competent young doctor everyone sees, and the hunted part of him that is still in the dark, waiting for the gunfire to start again.
